check:0:0.q: Why not “The token price, because it is on the monthly b…”?
check:0:0.a:
It gets one thing right. The token price is a real cost. It shows up on the monthly bill, so it is worth keeping an eye on.

But being visible is not the same as mattering. The lesson's **sensitivity analysis** (changing one guess at a time and watching how far the answer moves) shows the difference. Doubling the token price moves the monthly value by only about $390. Moving `success` (how often the AI is right) from 50 in 100 to 95 in 100 moves it by $18,900. That gap is the **swing**. The token price has a tiny swing, so even a bad surprise there will not sink the plan.

It is also the easy guess. You can look up the price on a pricing page. A trial that focuses on it measures the easy thing and misses the guess that could actually break the business case.

"How often the AI is right, on labelled past tickets" is better because it has by far the biggest swing, and testing on hand-labelled real tickets replaces that risky guess with a measured number.

judge.notes: No real problems. The one aside to watch is the 'look up the price on a pricing page' claim, which the lesson does not state, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The fixed monthly costs, because they come ever…”?
check:0:1.a:
That answer gets one thing right. Fixed costs really do come every month, and they are part of the plan. In the example, `fixed` is the 2300 taken off the monthly value.

But "every month" is not the test. The value here is a monthly value, so every guess in it repeats each month. The number of tasks, how often the AI is right and the saving per task all count again each month too. Repeating doesn't make one guess matter more than another.

What matters is the **swing**: how far the answer moves when you change that one guess from its bad value to its good value, keeping the others at their expected values. The question gives two swings. Token price moves the value by about $390. How often the AI is right moves it by $18,900. It gives no swing for fixed costs, so there is nothing to show they matter most. The option picks a guess for a reason that has nothing to do with swing.

"How often the AI is right, on labelled past tickets" is better because it has the biggest swing given, and checking hand-labelled tickets turns that guess into a measured number.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Nothing: two at a time is faster”?
check:1:0.a:
It does get one thing right. Moving two guesses together means fewer runs, so it is quicker.

But speed isn't the goal. The point of a sensitivity analysis is to find *which* guess moves the answer most, so you know what to measure hardest in the trial. When two guesses move at once, you get one combined change. You can't split it back into "this much from task count" and "this much from success."

Try it with the HR numbers. At the base case (6,000 tasks, `success` 0.8), the value is about $31,300. Now drop tasks to 4,000 *and* `success` to 0.5 together. The value falls to about $11,700, a drop of $19,600. Was that mostly task count? Mostly `success`? The single number can't tell you.

Moving one guess at a time keeps the others fixed. So any change in the answer belongs to that one guess alone. That is what makes the swings fair to compare.

"You can't tell which guess moved it" is better because it names the real cost: you lose the very information the analysis exists to find.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The HR arithmetic checks out ($31,300 base; $11,700 with tasks at 4,000 and success at 0.5; a $19,600 drop). The 4,000 task count is an illustrative value that the lesson does not give, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:1:1.q: Why not “They should move every guess at once”?
check:1:1.a:
Moving every guess at once isn't useless. It shows you the whole plan's worst or best outcome: "if everything goes wrong, what's left?" That's a fair question to ask once.

But it can't answer the question a sensitivity analysis is for: which single guess matters most? When two or more guesses move together, their effects get tangled. The answer shifts, and you can't split the blame.

Take the HR plan. Drop `success` to 0.5 and halve the task count to 3,000, both at once. The monthly value falls from about $31,300 to $8,200. That's a drop of about $23,100. How much came from `success`, and how much from the task count? You can't tell from that one result.

Now move one guess at a time, keeping the others at their base values. Each guess gets its own **swing**, meaning how far the answer moves. You compare the swings and see which guess deserves the hardest measuring, like the 50 hand-labelled tickets for `success`.

"You can't tell which guess moved it" is better because it names the real problem: mixing changes hides the cause, so the trial might measure the wrong thing.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Ask staff how good they think it will be”?
check:2:1.a:
Asking staff is cheap, and it isn't useless. Staff know the tickets well. They can warn you about tricky cases, and asking them helps get them on board.

But their answer is still a **guess**, not a measurement. Nobody has watched the AI answer a real ticket yet. People tend to be too hopeful about new tools, or too doubtful. Either way, you'd swap one guess for another.

That matters here because this guess has the biggest **swing**. The value could land anywhere from $11,000 to $29,900 a month depending on how often the AI is right. The guess that moves the answer most is the one that most needs real evidence. An opinion can't narrow that range much.

Trying the prompt on 50 past tickets labelled by hand is better because it measures what the AI actually does on real work, cheaply, before you build the whole bot. "Labelled by hand" means a person has written the correct answer for each ticket, so you can check the AI against it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Read the model maker's benchmark scores”?
check:2:2.a:
Reading the model maker's benchmark scores is cheap, and it does tell you something real. A **benchmark** is a fixed set of test questions the maker runs their model on. A high score means the model is generally capable.

But the guess you need is narrower. It is how often *your* bot gets *your* HR tickets right. Benchmarks test general tasks like maths puzzles or trivia. They don't test your company's leave policy, your ticket wording, or your prompt. The maker also picks which scores to publish, so they tend to look good.

That gap matters here. This guess swings the value from $11,000 to $29,900. A borrowed number could leave you confidently wrong on the guess that decides the plan.

Trying the prompt on 50 past tickets labelled by hand is better. It is still cheap, and it measures the exact thing the `success` guess stands for: your prompt, on your real tickets, checked against answers you trust.

judge.notes: No check fails. The remark that makers pick which scores to publish goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Move one guess, keep the biggest” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "A business case rests on guesses: how many tasks, how often the AI is right, and how much each task saves. A trial can't measure all of them well. So I need to know which guess matters most."

*The idea:* "I run a sensitivity analysis. I move one guess from its worst case to its best case and keep the others at their expected values. The gap between the two results is the swing. The guess with the biggest swing is the one I measure hardest. In an HR example, the AI's success rate swung the monthly value by about $18,900. Doubling the token price moved it by only about $390."

*A trade-off:* "Moving one guess at a time misses guesses that move together. Say fewer tickets also means harder tickets. Then the real worst case is worse than either swing alone."

**A likely follow-up**

"Where do the low and high values come from?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* You agree them with the business owner up front. Then you replace the top guess with a real measurement. For example, you score the prompt on 50 hand-labelled past tickets with MLflow.

judge.notes: No real problems. The trade-off about guesses that move together is not in the lesson, but it does not contradict it. The answer is about 196 words, just under the limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The plan misses in real use, and nobody knows why.** The business case promised about $31,300 a month. Real results come in far lower. Often the culprit is a guess that was never tested.
- **Effort went to the small guesses.** The team checked token prices carefully, which move the answer by a few hundred dollars. Meanwhile `success`, how often the AI is right, was still a hopeful round number like 0.8.
- **Several guesses changed at once.** If you move two guesses together, you can't tell which one caused the change in value.
- **Ranges that are too narrow.** A guess looks unimportant if its bad and good values were set almost the same. Check whether the owner really agreed those limits.
- **Ranking by a negative swing.** If a swing comes out below zero and isn't made positive, the order of the guesses is wrong.

**Quickest check**

Make a short list of every guess. Next to each one, write its swing and whether its number was **measured** (for example, from 50 hand-labelled tickets) or just **assumed**. If the guess at the top of the list is still only assumed, you've found the problem. Measure that one first.

judge.notes: No significant problems. It is close to the 200-word limit (about 197 words), and the 'negative swing' bullet only hints at the abs step without giving the solution.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Guesses that move together.** The method changes one guess at a time, but some guesses are linked. If the AI is often wrong, staff may spend extra time fixing its answers, so `success` and saving both fall at once. Also try a few combined scenarios, such as everything at its worst case, to see the true downside.

**2. Things change over time.** Your measured `success` comes from past tickets, and new ticket types, policy changes or a model update can shift it. Re-run the evaluation on freshly labelled tickets regularly and update the plan when the share moves.

**3. Very little labelled data.** With only 50 tickets, a measured share of 80 in 100 could really be a fair bit higher or lower. Treat that measurement as a range and use its edges as your new low and high. If the swing is still the biggest, label more tickets before you trust it.

learn:term.q: How is “worst case” different from “base case”?
learn:term.a:
The **base case** is your expected value for a guess: the number you'd bet on if you had to pick one. The **worst case** is the bad but still believable value: what you'd see if things go poorly.

Think of planning a commute. Base case: it usually takes 30 minutes. Worst case: on a rainy day with roadworks, 50 minutes. Both are real possibilities. One is typical, the other is the bad end.

In the lesson, the `success` guess (how often the AI is right) has a base case of 0.8 and a worst case of 0.5. With everything else at base, the monthly value is about $31,300 at 0.8. At 0.5 it drops to about $18,700.

They work together in a sensitivity analysis. You move one guess to its worst case (and then its best case) while every other guess stays at its base case. Holding the rest at base means any change in the answer comes from that one guess alone. The gap between the worst-case and best-case answers is that guess's **swing**.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The cheaper model still sends the same number o…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option has a grain of truth. A cheaper model may well use about the same number of **tokens** (the chunks of text a model reads and writes). But that fact doesn't explain the result. It actually points the other way.

If the tokens stay the same and the price per token halves, the model's bill halves too. In the HR ticket example, it drops from 6.5 cents to about 3.25 cents. That is a real cut to the model's part.

So why does the cost per finished task hardly move? Because the model was never the big part. The other two parts stay the same:

- **Human review** (a person checking some answers) costs 60 cents a ticket.
- **Rework** (redoing the answers that fail) costs $1.20 a ticket.

Halving the token price saves about 3 cents out of $1.865. That's under 2 percent of the total.

The tokens option only looks at the model's bill. It misses the costs that sit around it.

"Checking and redoing answers cost far more than tokens" is better because it names the real reason: the model is under 4 percent of the fully loaded cost, so even halving it barely changes the total.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Token prices only count for answers, not for pr…”?
check:0:1.a:
**Why "Token prices only count for answers, not for prompts" is not the best answer**

It gets one thing right: answer tokens often cost more each than prompt tokens. But the claim itself is false. You pay for both. A **token** is a small chunk of text the model reads or writes. The lesson's MLflow code charges for both kinds: `input_tokens` (the prompt) at `IN`, and `output_tokens` (the answer) at `OUT`.

It also misses the real reason. Even if only answers were charged, halving the token price would still cut that bill in half. So it can't explain why the total hardly moves.

Here is what really happens. In the HR ticket example, tokens cost 6.5 cents out of $1.865. Halving that saves about 3 cents, so the total becomes roughly $1.83. The 60 cents for checking and the $1.20 for redoing don't change at all.

**Why the right option is better:** "Checking and redoing answers cost far more than tokens" names where the money goes. The model is under 4 percent of each finished ticket, so a cheaper model barely changes the total.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only small stretches are that the 'often cost more each' remark generalises from the lesson's example prices, and the closing explanation runs to two sentences instead of one.

check:1:0.a:
The price list is a real source, just for a different number. It tells you what the model charges per token. A token is a small chunk of text, roughly part of a word. You need that figure for the model's share of the bill, the 6.5 cents in the HR ticket example.

But the price list only knows about the model. It says nothing about people. How long a person spends checking one answer depends on the team, the kind of ticket, and how careful the checks need to be. No model vendor can know that.

It also matters because checking is a big part of the cost. In the example, checking adds 60 cents a ticket. That is far more than the model's 6.5 cents. If you guessed the check time from the wrong source, your whole estimate would be off.

So each number comes from whoever actually knows it. The price list gives token prices. The trial build gives token counts and failure rates.

The owner of the use case is better because they run the real work, so they know how long a check takes and how many answers get checked.

check:1:2.a:
It's a fair guess. Traces are real measurements, and the lesson does use them. A **trace** is a step-by-step record of one run of your AI app: what went in, what came out, and how many tokens the model used. That makes traces the right source for the model's bill.

But a trace only sees what happens inside the software. It stops when the answer is produced. The person who reads that answer and checks it works outside the app. Their two minutes never show up in any trace. The lesson's own code says this too: "Checking and redo costs come from the POC's review notes, not traces."

There's a second gap. How long a check takes depends on how the team plans to work. For example, how careful must a reviewer be with HR answers? That is a business choice, not something software can measure.

**The owner of the use case is better because they run the team doing the checking, so they know how long a check takes and can stand behind that number.**

judge.notes: The claim that the owner 'runs the team doing the checking' and that check time is a 'business choice' goes beyond the lesson, which only says the owner supplies the check time, but it does not contradict it.

check:2:1.q: Why not “It stays the same: tokens didn't change”?
check:2:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. The tokens didn't change, so the model's bill per task stays the same.

But the model's bill is only one part. The **cost per finished task** adds up three things:

- the model's tokens
- **human review**: a person checking some answers
- **rework**: redoing the answers that fail

The prompt fix doesn't touch the tokens. It does touch rework. Before, 1 in 5 answers failed, which is 20 in 100. After the fix, only 10 in 100 fail. So half as many answers need redoing.

Say each redo costs $8, like the HR ticket example:

- before: 0.20 × $8 = $1.60 of rework per task
- after: 0.10 × $8 = $0.80 of rework per task

That's 80 cents saved on every task, with no change to the model's bill. The HR example also showed the model was under 4 percent of the total. So looking only at tokens misses most of the cost.

"It goes down: less rework to pay for" is better because fewer failures mean fewer redos, and redos are part of what a finished task costs.

check:2:2.q: Why not “It goes up: fixes always cost more”?
check:2:2.a:
"It goes up: fixes always cost more" gets one thing right. Making a fix is not free. Someone spends time rewriting the prompt (the instructions you give the model). And some fixes do add cost, like a longer prompt that uses more tokens.

But this question rules that out. It says the tokens stay the same, so the model's bill per task does not change. The person's time to write the fix is paid once. It is not paid again on every ticket.

What the answer misses is rework, meaning redoing the answers that fail. Rework is often the biggest part of the cost per finished task. Say each redo costs $8, as in the HR ticket bot:

- 1 in 5 fail: 0.2 × $8 = $1.60 a task
- Half as many fail: 0.1 × $8 = $0.80 a task

That saves 80 cents on every ticket. The model's bill is only a few cents, so this saving is far bigger.

"It goes down: less rework to pay for" is better because the tokens stay the same while failures are halved, so the rework cost on every task drops by half.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Add checking and redoing to the cost” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
The token bill is the number that shows up on the invoice, so it's tempting to stop there. But a finished task also needs people. Someone checks some answers. That is **human review**. Someone redoes the ones that fail. That is **rework**. Their time costs real money, and it is usually far bigger than the token bill.

If you skip it, the project looks much cheaper than it is. It gets approved and built. Then the real costs arrive, the budget breaks, and the project gets dropped. That is part of why Gartner expected many AI trials to be abandoned.

**A small example.** An HR ticket costs $8 by hand today. The model's tokens cost 6.5 cents. Compare just those, and you seem to save almost $8 a ticket.

Now add the people:

- Checking 30 in 100 answers adds 60 cents.
- Redoing the 15 in 100 that fail adds $1.20.

The real cost is about $1.87. You still save, but about $6.13 a ticket, not $7.94. Over 10,000 tickets a month, your forecast was $18,000 too rosy.

Pricing this way also tells your trial what to measure: how often answers fail, and how long a check takes.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Add up the three costs” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "Teams often price an AI task by the model's token bill alone. That hides most of the real cost. Rising costs and unclear value are one reason many AI projects get dropped after the trial stage."

*The idea:* "So I price a **finished** task. I add up three costs: the model's tokens, a person checking some answers (human review), and redoing the answers that fail (rework). In an HR ticket bot, the tokens were 6.5 cents. The full cost was about $1.87, so the model was under 4 percent."

*An edge case:* "Mistakes nobody catches cost extra too. I keep those apart and take them off the saving later, so nothing gets counted twice."

**A likely follow-up**

"Where does each number come from?"

*Hint:* Name a source for each one. The price list gives token prices. The POC (proof of concept, a small trial build) measures token use and how often answers fail. The use-case owner, often the product manager, gives the hourly rate, today's cost of a task, how many answers get checked, and how long a check takes. A strong answer shows you priced the task first, so you knew what the trial had to measure.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
## Warning signs

**The plan quotes only the token bill.** If your cost estimate is a few cents a task, people's time is probably missing. In the HR bot, tokens are 6.5 cents of $1.865.

**The saving shrinks in real use.** On paper you save about $7.94 a ticket. Then reviewers log hours and failed answers get redone by hand, and the real saving is far smaller.

**The trial didn't record the right things.** If the POC (proof of concept, the small trial build) never noted how many answers were checked, how long checks took, or how many failed, those costs are guesses.

**A number has no source.** Each input should trace back to the price list, the POC, or the use case owner.

**Uncaught mistakes are counted twice.** If the 50 cents is in the cost and is also taken off the saving, your payback looks worse than it really is.

## Quickest check

Take one week of finished tasks. Add the model bill, the review hours times the hourly rate, and the redo count times the cost of a redo. Divide by the number of tasks. If that is far above your planned figure, a cost was left out.

judge.notes: No major problem; the $7.94 'on paper' saving is not in the lesson and is only the $8 hand cost minus tokens (the full-cost saving is $6.135), and the answer is about 200 words, right at the length limit.

learn:stops.a:
**The failure rate drifts over time.** The 15 in 100 failure share comes from the POC (proof of concept, a small trial build), but real tickets change after launch. New policies or new kinds of questions can push failures up. Re-measure how often answers fail, and how many get checked, every month or so, and reprice.

**An agent takes a different number of steps each time.** Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and you pay for each one. An agent that loops or calls tools may use ten times more tokens on hard tasks, so one average hides the costly cases. Look at the spread of cost per task, not just the average, and price the expensive end too.

**The trial was tiny.** If the POC ran only 20 tickets, a measured failure share of 15 in 100 could really be 5 or 30. Price a low, a middle and a high case instead of one number. Then run a bigger trial before you commit.

judge.notes: The question asks for two or three sentences per situation, but each of the three situations runs to four sentences.

learn:term.q: How is “fully loaded cost” different from “human review”?
learn:term.a:
They sit at different levels. One is the whole bill. The other is one line on that bill.

**Fully loaded cost** is the full price of one finished task. It adds three parts: the model's token bill, plus human review, plus rework (redoing answers that fail).

**Human review** is just one of those parts. It is the cost of a person checking some of the answers. You work it out from three numbers: how many answers get checked, how long each check takes, and the person's hourly rate.

So human review feeds into the fully loaded cost. On its own, it is only part of the answer.

Think of a restaurant meal. The fully loaded cost is everything it takes to get the plate to the table. Human review is like the head chef tasting some dishes before they go out. It is a real cost, but only one piece.

In the lesson's HR ticket bot:

- Model: $0.065
- Human review: 30 in 100 checked, 2 minutes each, at $60 an hour, which comes to $0.60
- Rework: 15 in 100 redone at $8 each, which comes to $1.20
- Fully loaded cost: $1.865 a ticket

Human review alone is about a third of the total.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Global, because it is the cheapest”?
check:0:1.a:
"Global, because it is the cheapest" gets one thing right. Global really is the cheapest. For `gpt-4.1` in East US it costs $2.00 per million input tokens, against $2.20 for the others. (A token is a small chunk of text, roughly part of a word.)

What it misses is the rule. Global means your requests may be *processed* in any Azure region in the world. "Processed" means the place where the model actually reads your prompt and writes its answer. That could be outside the EU. So Global breaks the rule that the HR data must stay in the EU. It is out before price even comes up.

The catch is easy to miss. Your *stored* data stays in your chosen geography whichever type you pick. But the rule is also about where the work happens, not just where data is saved.

This is why the lesson says price comes last. First the rules remove options. Then you take the cheapest of what is left.

"Data Zone EU, or Regional in the EU" is better because it keeps processing inside the EU, so it follows the rule, and it costs only about 10% more.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Any type: stored data stays put”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. Stored data does stay in your chosen geography, whichever deployment type you pick. "Stored data" means things kept at rest, like saved files or logs.

But storage is only half the story. Each time your app sends a request, the model has to read your text and work on it. That step is called **processing**. The deployment type decides where processing may happen.

With **Global**, processing can happen in any Azure region in the world. So your HR data could briefly leave the EU while the model works on it, even though nothing is saved outside the EU. A rule like "must stay in the EU" usually covers processing too, not just storage. That is why Global is out, and why "any type" is wrong.

This is the first step of the lesson's order. Check the data rules before you look at price. Global is cheaper at $2.00 versus $2.20 per million input tokens, but it doesn't pass the rule.

"Data Zone EU, or Regional in the EU" is better because both keep processing inside the EU as well as storage.

judge.notes: No significant problems: the answer matches the lesson on storage versus processing, uses the lesson's prices, stays under about 200 words, and does not give away the exercise.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Use Global: it is only a test”?
check:1:1.a:
"Use Global: it is only a test" gets one thing right. Tests feel low-risk, and Global is often the only way to try a new model early. It is also the cheapest type. So the urge makes sense.

But it misses the main idea of the lesson. The data rule comes first, before price or convenience. Your rule says the data must stay in the EU. Global means your requests may be processed in any Azure region, including ones outside the EU. A "test" does not change that. The rule is about where the data goes, not about why you are sending it.

Tests also often use real data, like real HR records, because that's what you want to try the model on. If that data leaves the EU, you have broken the rule, even if it was "just a test." Your privacy team (the people who set data rules) would see it the same way.

"Wait for it in the EU Data Zone" is better because it follows the rule first and only then uses the model, once a version that keeps processing inside the EU is offered.

judge.notes: No major problem. The claim that tests often use real HR data goes beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it. The answer is also close to the 200-word limit.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Use Global, then delete the data”?
check:1:2.a:
**Why "Use Global, then delete the data" doesn't work**

It gets one thing right. Cleaning up data you no longer need is a good habit. And with any deployment type, your *stored* data already stays in your chosen geography.

But the rule is about where your data is *processed*. Processing means the model reading your prompt and writing its answer. With Global, that can happen in any Azure region, including outside the EU. So the moment you send a request, your data may already have left the EU. Deleting it afterwards can't undo that. The rule is broken during the request, not later.

It also skips the lesson's order. Your data rules come first. They decide which deployment types you may use at all. Global is out, so it never becomes an option, however new or cheap it is. A new model is a reason to wait, not a reason to bend the rule.

**Why "Wait for it in the EU Data Zone" is better:** a Data Zone EU deployment processes requests only inside the EU, so your data never leaves it.

check:2:1.a:
"$10 a month" gets one thing right. Data Zone does cost a little more than Global Standard, so the answer is a small extra cost, not zero.

What it misses is the size of the gap. Prices here are "per million tokens". A token is a small chunk of text, about part of a word. So first find the gap for one million tokens:

```
$2.20 - $2.00 = $0.20 per million input tokens
```

Then count how many millions you send. 500 million tokens is 500 lots of one million:

```
500 × $0.20 = $100 a month
```

"$10" usually comes from a slip somewhere. Maybe the gap was taken as $0.02, which is the embedding model's price, not gpt-4.1's. Or 500 million became 50 million. Or "about 10% more" turned into "$10 more". Each slip makes the answer ten times too small.

A habit that helps: find the gap per million, then multiply by the number of millions.

"$100 a month" is better because it multiplies the real $0.20 gap by all 500 millions of tokens.

check:2:2.a:
**Why not "$1,000 a month"?**

That number isn't random. It's what you get when you multiply 500 by $2.00. Prices are "per million tokens," and 500 million tokens is 500 of those millions. So $1,000 is the full monthly bill for **Global Standard**. You handled the units correctly, and that's the step people often get wrong.

The miss is the question itself. It doesn't ask what Global costs. It asks what Data Zone **adds**, meaning the extra you pay on top of Global.

Work out both bills, then take the gap:

```
# per month, 500 million input tokens
# Global:    500 × $2.00 = $1,000
# Data Zone: 500 × $2.20 = $1,100
# extra:     $1,100 − $1,000 = $100
```

There's a quicker way too. Data Zone costs $0.20 more per million tokens. Multiply that by 500 and you get $100.

**"$100 a month" is better because it's the difference between the two bills, which is exactly the extra cost of keeping processing inside one zone.**

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Filter by the rules, then take the cheapest” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:

learn:term.a:
A **deployment type** is a setting you choose when you set up a model in Azure AI Foundry. It decides **where in the world your requests may be processed**. "Processed" means the place where the model actually reads your prompt and writes its answer.

**An everyday comparison:** think of calling a help line. You could allow your call to be answered by staff anywhere in the world. That's the cheapest option. Or you could insist on staff in your continent only, or in your own country only. Those options cost a bit more. It's the same service, with different limits on location.

In the lesson, the three types are:

- **Global**: any Azure region. Cheapest.
- **Data Zone**: only inside one zone, such as the EU.
- **Regional (Standard)**: only inside the geography you choose.

Stored data stays in your chosen geography whichever type you pick. The type only limits where processing happens.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Only new documents use the new model”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a tempting answer because it sounds cheaper. And part of it is true: after the switch, new documents and every new question do go through the new model.

What it misses is that **vectors from two different models can't be compared.** Each model has its own way of turning meaning into numbers. A "close" match only makes sense when both vectors come from the same model. It's like measuring one wall in inches and another in centimetres, then asking which is longer by comparing the raw numbers.

So picture the index (the store of vectors the search looks through) after the change. The old HR documents still hold vectors from the old model. A new question gets a vector from the new model. The search would compare the two anyway, and the matches would be close to random. The old documents would quietly stop being found.

To keep search working, every document has to get a fresh vector from the new model.

"Every document is embedded again, once" is better because it names the real cost: one more full pass over all the documents, which you should put in the plan before swapping the model.

judge.notes: No real problems. The only stretch is 'close to random', which goes slightly past the lesson's 'can't be compared' but doesn't contradict it.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing: the old vectors still work”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing half right. The old vectors don't vanish. They still sit in the index, and searches against them still run. Nothing crashes.

What it misses is that every question gets turned into a vector by the *new* model. Each embedding model has its own way of placing meaning into numbers. Think of two maps of the same city drawn at different scales, with different starting points. A point on one map tells you nothing about the other.

So a new-model question vector compared against old-model document vectors gives junk matches. The search "works" in that it returns results, but they won't be the right ones. You can't mix the two models in one index.

The fix is to run every document through the new model, which is a full one-off cost again. For the HR assistant, that's another 3,000,000 tokens. After that, the monthly cost carries on as before.

"Every document is embedded again, once" is better because vectors from two different models can't be compared, so the whole index must be rebuilt with the new model before search gives sensible matches.

check:1:1.a:
"$1.50" is ten times too big. It has the right steps but loses a zero along the way.

**What it gets right:** the method. You multiply the questions by the tokens in each question. Then you multiply by the price.

**Where it slips:** the count and the division. Do it slowly:

1. **Count the tokens.** 300,000 questions × 25 tokens = 7,500,000 tokens. That is 7.5 million.
2. **Turn that into millions.** Divide by a million: 7.5.
3. **Times the price.** 7.5 × $0.02 = $0.15.

To get $1.50, you would need 75 million tokens. That is ten times more than the questions really use. Or you would need a price of $0.20 a million instead of $0.02. Both are easy slips when a sum has this many zeros.

A quick sense check helps. One million tokens costs two cents. Seven and a half million should cost about fifteen cents, not a dollar and a half.

**Why "$0.15" is better:** it is 7.5 million tokens times $0.02 a million, with every zero kept in its place.

check:1:2.a:
"$150" gets the first step right. It counts the tokens correctly: 300,000 questions times 25 tokens is 7,500,000 tokens a month.

The slip is in the last step. The price is $0.02 per **million** tokens. "$150" comes from treating it as $0.02 per **thousand** tokens. That means dividing by 1,000 instead of 1,000,000. The answer ends up a thousand times too big.

Here is the sum done the lesson's way:

```python
tokens = 300000 * 25            # 7,500,000 tokens
cost = tokens * 0.02 / 1000000  # $0.15
```

A quick sense check helps here. Embeddings are cheap, and the lesson's whole HR library cost only $0.06 to embed. So $150 a month for short questions should feel wrong straight away.

"$0.15" is better because it counts 7.5 million tokens and charges them at $0.02 for each million, just as the price says.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Embedding the documents the first time”?
check:2:1.a:
"Embedding the documents the first time" is a real cost, so that part is right. Before a RAG app can search anything, every chunk of every document has to become a vector (a list of numbers that captures meaning). That builds the index, the store the search looks through.

But the question asks which cost is *easiest to forget*. The first pass is hard to forget. You can't launch without it. It sits right at the start of the plan, where everyone looks. In the HR example it is the obvious line: 3,000,000 tokens, $0.06, once.

The cost people miss is the one that shows up later. Someone swaps in a newer embedding model to get better matches. Vectors from two different models can't be compared. So every document must be embedded again, a full second pass. That happens long after launch, and it looks like a simple upgrade. So nobody budgets for it.

"Embedding everything again after a model change" is the better answer. It is a full-size cost hidden behind a decision that sounds small, so it rarely makes it into the plan.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Embedding new documents each month”?
check:2:2.a:
Embedding new documents each month is a real cost. That part is right. Every new HR document has to become a vector, a list of numbers, before search can find it. So it belongs in the plan.

But it is not the easiest cost to forget. It is regular. It shows up every month, so it sits in the monthly budget next to the cost of embedding every question. It is also small. In the lesson's example, 100 new documents add only 150,000 tokens, part of the "about $0.02 a month."

Re-embedding is different. It only happens when someone decides to switch to a newer embedding model. Vectors from two different models can't be compared. So every document has to be embedded again, a full second pass. In the example, that is another 3,000,000 tokens. Nobody thinks about it on day one, because no swap is planned yet.

"Embedding everything again after a model change" is the better answer because it is a one-off, full-size cost that only appears later, so it is the one most plans leave out.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Tokens times the price, once and every month” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "A RAG app looks up documents before it answers. To search by meaning, it turns text into vectors, which are lists of numbers. Every chunk of every document gets embedded, and so does every question. Each one is billed per token, the small pieces of words a model counts."

*The idea:* "So I count the tokens and multiply by the price per token. I pay once for all the documents when I build the index. Then I pay every month for new documents plus every question. For 2,000 HR documents that's about six cents once, then about two cents a month."

*The trade-off:* "A newer embedding model may find better matches. But vectors from two models can't be compared. So every document has to be embedded again. I put that full pass in the plan before anyone swaps the model."

**A likely follow-up**

"If embeddings are this cheap, where does the real cost sit?"

*Hint:* Say embeddings are rarely the big line on the bill. The search service that stores the vectors usually costs much more.

judge.notes: The answer matches the lesson. The only small stretch is the hint's 'much more', where the lesson says only that the search service 'usually' is the big line.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **An estimate that is wildly off.** If your one-off cost comes out near $60,000 instead of $0.06, the price per million was never turned into a price per token. If it comes out as a tiny fraction of a cent, you divided twice.
- **A monthly bill higher than planned.** Often the questions were left out. Each question becomes a vector before the search, so it costs tokens too.
- **A surprise one-off spike.** Someone swapped the embedding model, and every document was embedded again. Nobody had put that full pass in the plan.
- **Search that suddenly gets worse.** The model changed, but only new documents were re-embedded. Now old and new vectors (the lists of numbers) come from two models. They can't be compared, so matches look random.

**Quickest check**

Redo the sum by hand for one month: new documents' tokens plus the questions' tokens, times the price per million, divided by a million. Compare it with the usage page in your billing portal.

Then confirm that every vector in the index was made by the same embedding model.

learn:stops.a:
The simple sum, tokens times the price, works well for small, steady apps. Here are three places it needs extra care.

**Documents get edited, not just added.** The lesson counts only new documents each month. If policies are rewritten often, every changed chunk must be embedded again. Count edited chunks in the monthly total, not just new ones.

**Chunks overlap.** Many apps let each chunk repeat a little of the one before, so no sentence gets cut in half. That repeated text is embedded twice. Your token count can then be noticeably higher than the raw document size. Count tokens after chunking, not before.

**You pay by the hour, not by the token.** Some Databricks endpoints use **provisioned throughput**. That means you reserve capacity and pay for every hour it runs, busy or idle. Then the cost is hours times the hourly rate. At very large scale, also check **rate limits**, the cap on how fast you may send text. Re-embedding millions of documents can take days.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. Each situation runs over the requested two or three sentences, and the provisioned-throughput and rate-limit points go beyond the lesson without contradicting it.

learn:term.a:
An **embedding** is the act of turning text into numbers. A **vector** is the result: the list of numbers itself.

So embedding is the step, and the vector is what comes out of it. People also say "an embedding" to mean the vector it made, so the two words often blur together.

**An everyday comparison.** Think of taking a photo. Taking the photo is the embedding. The photo you hold afterwards is the vector. You pay for the camera work, and then you keep the photo.

**How they work together in the HR assistant:**

- Each chunk of the 2,000 HR documents goes through an embedding model. Each chunk comes out as a vector.
- When someone asks a question, the question is embedded too. That gives one more vector.
- The search compares the question's vector with the stored vectors and finds the closest meanings.

**Where the cost sits.** The embedding step is billed per token. That is the $0.06 once and about $0.02 a month. The vectors are what you store. Holding them is the search service's job, which the next lesson covers.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The name of the person who typed it”?
check:0:1.a:
Knowing who typed the line isn't useless. It gives you someone to ask. In a team, that can help.

But it doesn't solve the real problem. The lesson's point is that pricing pages change. A line like "web search: $14 per 1,000" is only true for a while. To trust it, you need to answer two questions:

- **Is this number still right?** A name can't tell you. You'd have to find that person and hope they remember. They might have left the company. They might have copied the number from somewhere else.
- **Where can I check it?** A name gives you nowhere to look.

The page and the date answer both questions. The page lets anyone open it and see today's price. The date tells you how old the number is, so you know when it might be stale and needs updating.

A good line looks like this:

```
web search: $14 per 1,000 (source: provider's pricing page, checked 2025-06-01)
```

"The page it came from, and the date" is better because it lets anyone check the number themselves and spot when it's out of date, without depending on one person.

check:0:2.q: Why not “A note saying prices never change”?
check:0:2.a:
That note would say something false. The lesson's first point is that pricing pages change. Providers raise prices, cut them, and rename products. A line that says "this never changes" tells the next reader to trust a number that may already be out of date.

It does get one thing right. It shows the writer was thinking about whether the price will hold. That is the right worry. It just gives the wrong answer to it.

It also misses what the line actually needs. Picture someone opening your worksheet six months from now. They see "$14 per 1,000" and wonder if it's still true. A "never changes" note gives them nowhere to look and no way to tell how old the number is. So they can't check it, and they won't know when to update it.

That matters when you compare your estimate to the real bill. If web search comes in at 3 times the plan, you want to know whether the price changed or your usage did.

"The page it came from, and the date" is better because it lets anyone go back to the source, check the number, and update it when the page changes.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that providers 'rename products' goes slightly beyond the lesson, but it does not contradict it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “One region is always faster”?
check:1:1.a:
**Why "One region is always faster" is not the best answer**

There is a grain of truth in it. A **region** is one group of data centers in one place, like US East. If that region is close to your users, requests travel a shorter distance, so answers can come back a bit quicker. That delay is called **latency**.

The trouble is the word "always." A **Global deployment** sends each request to whichever data center has spare room at that moment. Often that is fast too. A single region can also be slower if it is busy, or if it sits far from your users. Speed depends on distance and load. Picking one region does not guarantee it.

It also misses the bigger point. A 10% higher price is usually worth paying for a firm rule, not for a speed boost that may or may not show up.

**Why "Your data must stay in that region" is better:** laws, contracts or company policy can require that your data is processed in one place, and a Global deployment may send it elsewhere, so the region is the only option that follows the rule.

judge.notes: No real problems. The description of how Global deployments route requests goes beyond the lesson, but it is accurate and doesn't contradict it, and the answer stays just under the length limit.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Global prices change every day”?
check:1:2.a:
"Global prices change every day" doesn't answer the question. The question asks why you would pay more on purpose: $0.022 instead of $0.02.

**What it gets right:** prices do change. The lesson says pricing pages change, which is why you write down the source and the date next to every price.

**What it misses:** that is true of every price, the region's included. The lesson never says Global prices move more often than others. Global is just one of the tiers it lists, next to Batch and reserved. And even if a price moved, that tells you to re-check it, not to pay 10% more forever. A changing price isn't a reason to pick the region.

The real reason has nothing to do with cost. Some companies have rules, often called *data residency* rules, that say certain data must stay in a certain place. If your data has to stay in one region, the cheaper option may simply not be allowed.

"Your data must stay in that region" is better because it gives a real requirement that outweighs a small price difference.

check:2:1.a:
The pricing calculator is a good tool, just for a different moment. It helps you **plan**. You type in how much you expect to use, and it multiplies that by the list price. That is exactly the "turn it into one task" step from earlier in this lesson.

But the question asks what your feature **really cost last month**. The calculator can't answer that, for two reasons:

- **It doesn't know what you actually used.** It only knows the numbers you typed in. If your agent ran three times as many web searches as planned, the calculator never sees it.
- **It shows list prices.** "List price" means the public price on the page. It leaves out your company's agreement, your currency and your tier, such as batch or reserved.

So the calculator gives you an estimate, not a bill.

The `system.billing.usage` table is better because Databricks records what your workloads actually used in it. It lists the DBUs (Databricks Units, what Databricks bills by) by product and by day. That gives you the real usage to check your estimate against.

judge.notes: Minor: the detail 'by product and by day' about the usage table is not in the lesson, and the 'why it is better' part runs to three sentences instead of one.

check:2:2.a:
The model's documentation is a fair place to learn what a model can do. Some docs even mention a price per million tokens. So it isn't useless.

But the question asks what your feature **really cost last month**. Documentation can't answer that. It doesn't know how many tokens your feature actually used. It doesn't know your company's agreed rate, your region, or your tier. At best it gives a list price. A list price is the standard number on the page, before any deals or differences.

The docs are also the wrong kind of source. They describe the model in general. They don't record what happened in your account.

That gap matters. The lesson's web search example was planned at $210 but billed at $630. Only the real bill shows a gap like that.

The `system.billing.usage` table is better because it is Databricks' own record of what your account actually used and was billed for. It's a built-in "system table", meaning one Databricks fills in for you automatically.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only weak spot is the claim that some docs mention a price per million tokens, which the lesson does not say but does not contradict.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Price per unit, times the units one task uses” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* Providers price things in different units. Tokens come by the million, searches by the thousand, and Databricks bills by the DBU (Databricks Unit, its own billing measure). You can't budget until they all mean the same thing.

*The idea:* I turn every price into the cost of one finished task. For each line, I divide the price by its unit size and multiply by how much one task uses. Then I add the lines up. It's like costing a recipe: flour is sold by the kilo, but I only use 200 grams. I note the source and date next to each price so anyone can check it.

*The trade-off:* The page shows a list price. My company's agreement, our region or a batch tier can change it. So it stays an estimate until I compare it with the real bill.

**A likely follow-up**

"You planned $210 for web search, but the bill says $630. What do you do?"

*Hint:* Find which line is off first. Then check the traces, which are logs of each step the agent took. They show whether tasks use more searches than you planned.

judge.notes: No major problems. The definition of traces as logs of each agent step is not in the lesson, but it does not contradict it.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
The clearest sign is a gap between your estimate and the real bill. Once the system is live, put each planned line next to what you were billed. A small gap is normal. A big one means a step was skipped.

**Common warning signs:**

- **Off by exactly 1,000 or 1,000,000.** You probably misread the unit. For example, you treated "per million tokens" as "per 1,000 tokens."
- **Steadily a bit higher or lower.** You likely used the list price. That is the public price before any company discount. Your company's agreed rate, region or tier may differ.
- **Fine at first, wrong months later.** The pricing page changed. With no source and date written down, nobody knew to update the estimate.
- **One line far over plan,** like web search at 3 times the estimate. A task uses more than you assumed. Check the traces, the step-by-step records of what each task did.

**Quickest check:** pick one line and redo it by hand. Read the unit on the pricing page again. Then compare the total with Azure Cost Management, or on Databricks with the `system.billing.usage` table.

learn:stops.a:
**When "price per unit, times units per task" stops working**

**1. Tasks don't all use the same amount.**
An agent may loop, retry, or call a tool several times on hard questions. One "average" task hides the expensive ones. Look at your traces (the step-by-step logs of each run), find a typical task and a heavy one, and price both.

**2. Some costs are paid by the hour, not by the task.**
A serving endpoint or `AI Search Standard` bills every hour it is running, even when nobody uses it. Work out the cost per hour, then divide it by how many tasks you expect in that hour. With little traffic, each task becomes much more expensive than the per-unit maths suggests.

**3. The price per unit isn't one fixed number.**
Volume discounts, free allowances, cheaper cached tokens (input the model has already seen recently) and batch tiers all change the rate. Ask your buyer for the real rate. Then check your estimate against `system.billing.usage` or Azure Cost Management once real usage arrives.

judge.notes: No real problem. Volume discounts, free allowances and cached tokens aren't in the lesson, but they don't contradict it.

learn:term.a:
Without this, cost estimates are guesses that look like facts.

Picture a team planning an agent that runs 100,000 tasks a month, each using half a web search. Someone reads the price as "$14 per million searches" instead of "$14 per 1,000". Their plan says about $0.70 a month for search. The real cost is $700. Nobody catches it, because the plan has no source and no date. No one can check where the $14 came from.

Each of the lesson's four steps blocks a mistake like that:

- **Find the page:** the number comes from the provider, not from memory or an old blog post.
- **Read the unit:** per million tokens, per 1,000 searches, per hour, or per DBU (Databricks Unit, the measure Databricks bills by).
- **Turn it into one task:** you see what a single run costs, so you can multiply by how many runs you expect.
- **Write the source and the date:** anyone can recheck the number when the page changes.

Separately, after launch, you compare the estimate with the real bill. A line at 3 times the plan tells you where to look.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Ask Claude in the instructions to add up the co…”?
check:0:0.a:
Asking Claude to "add up the costs carefully" gets one thing right. It puts the requirement in the instructions, so Claude knows a total is needed. That part is good.

What it misses is that the word "carefully" doesn't change how Claude works. Claude is a language model. It writes answers by predicting likely text, not by doing exact arithmetic the way a calculator does. Most of the time the sum will be right. Sometimes a number will be slightly off, and it may come out different on two runs with the same inputs. You can't easily tell which runs went wrong.

The total cost of ownership (every cost of running the idea over time, added up) is exactly the kind of figure people make decisions on. One wrong digit there matters.

That is why this skill ships with `scripts/tco.py`. Claude passes it the inputs, the script does the maths, and Claude reports the table it prints.

**Why the script wins:** a script gives the same correct total every time for the same inputs, and you can test it once and trust it.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Write the current prices into the description”?
check:0:2.a:
Putting prices into the description has one good instinct: real numbers are better than guesses. But it puts them in the wrong place and still leaves the hard part undone.

First, the description has a different job. Claude reads the name and description of every skill up front to decide *whether* to use it. It is a short "what this does and when to use it" note, capped at 1,024 characters. A price list there crowds out the words that help Claude pick your skill at the right moment.

Second, it doesn't make the answer reliable. Even with the right prices, Claude would still add up the total cost of ownership (all the costs of running the system over time) in its head. A model can get sums wrong.

Third, prices change. Numbers baked into a description go stale quietly.

The right answer is better because a script like `scripts/tco.py` does the arithmetic the same way every time, so the total is exact, and the skill just runs it and reports the table.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The script that adds up costs”?
check:1:0.a:
The cost script is a sensible thing to check, just not first. It is the right place for exact sums, because a model can add numbers wrong and a script cannot. If your cost table came out wrong, `scripts/tco.py` would be the first suspect.

But look at the problem. Claude never uses the skill at all. The script only runs at step 8, after Claude has already picked the skill and started following its steps. So the script never gets a chance to run. Fixing it cannot change whether the skill is chosen.

Here is how choosing works. Up front, Claude reads only the `name` and `description` of every skill. It loads the rest of `SKILL.md` only when a request matches. If the `description` never says something like "Use when someone asks whether an AI idea is worth doing", Claude has no reason to pick it.

"The description: when to use it" is better because, of the two settings Claude reads before choosing, the `description` is the one that says when the skill applies, so it decides whether the skill is ever used.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The output format at the end”?
check:1:1.a:
The output format is a real part of a good skill. It tells Claude what the finished answer should look like, such as the cost table and a clear verdict. If that part were vague, you would get messy or uneven results.

But that only matters once the skill is running. The problem here comes earlier: Claude never uses the skill at all.

Remember how Claude finds skills. Up front, it reads only two things from every skill: the `name` and the `description` in the frontmatter (the settings between the `---` markers). The body, including the output format, loads only after a request matches. So Claude never even sees the output format until it has already picked the skill. Fixing it cannot help Claude pick it.

The `description: when to use it` is the better answer. The name is mostly a label, so the description is what Claude compares against your request. It must say what the skill does and when to use it, for example "Use when someone asks whether an AI idea is worth doing."

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Check the rules, then write the file” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* A Claude skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file. Claude reads its name and description first. If those break the rules, the skill will not load.

*The idea.* So I check before I write. I gather every rule the input breaks and report them all together. Only when nothing is wrong do I build the file. That means the frontmatter (the settings between `---` markers), then a title, then numbered steps. It's like a form that is checked before it is sent.

*The trade-off.* Collecting every problem takes a little more code than stopping at the first one. But the person can fix everything in one pass instead of retrying again and again.

**Likely follow-up:** "Why not just write the file and fix problems later?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Catching mistakes when the file is created is cheaper than finding out later that the skill would not load. You could add that passing the rules isn't the whole job. The description also decides whether Claude ever picks the skill, so a valid but vague description is still a risk.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs your skill is broken or never ran**

- **It never kicks in.** You ask Claude to assess an AI idea, and it answers in its own loose way. There is no one-line use case, no gates, no cost table. Usually the description is too vague. Or the file broke a rule, so Claude never saw the skill at all.
- **The answers drift.** Two similar ideas come back in different shapes, with steps missing or reordered. A skill is meant to make the routine identical every time.
- **The cost totals wobble.** The same inputs give slightly different totals, or the rows don't add up. That means the model did the sums itself instead of running `scripts/tco.py`.
- **Known gaps slip through.** You feed it an idea with an obvious hole, like no acceptance criteria, and it passes anyway.

**Quickest check**

Open a fresh Claude Code session and type `/vet-ai-use-case`. If it isn't offered, the skill didn't load, so recheck the frontmatter (the settings between the `---` markers). If it loads, run one idea whose gaps you already know. Then compare its cost table with what `tco.py` prints when you run it yourself on the same inputs.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The description is vague or overlaps another skill.** Claude reads only the name and description up front, so a fuzzy description means your skill never loads, or a similar one loads instead. Name the exact trigger, like "when someone asks whether an AI idea is worth doing," and test it with real requests.

**2. The facts behind the routine change over time.** Prices, approved models and company rules shift, and a skill written once quietly goes out of date. Keep changing numbers in a separate reference file or in the inputs the script reads. Then review the skill on a schedule.

**3. The routine grows very large.** A huge SKILL.md is slow to load and hard for Claude to follow, and different teams may vet ideas differently. Keep the main steps short. Move details into reference files that Claude opens only when needed, or split the routine into several smaller skills.

In every case, test it the same way the lesson says. Run the skill on ideas with known problems, see what it misses, and fix the instructions.

explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

I also read each document once, when it arrives, with the cheapest service that does the job.

**A likely follow-up**

"When would you pay $10 per 1,000 pages instead of $1.50?"

*Hint:* Only when you need tables or layout. Plain text reading is enough otherwise. Also note that reading each document once makes it a one-time cost. For 20,000 pages that's $200 once, not every month.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

The first sign is usually the bill. Your token costs look fine, but the monthly invoice is much higher than you planned. When you split it by service, search or Document Intelligence (Azure's page-reading service) is bigger than the model itself.

In your traces, look for these. A trace is the step-by-step record of what the agent did for one question.

- One question triggers three, five or ten searches when you assumed one.
- The same document gets read again on every question instead of once when it arrived.
- Every page goes through Layout at $10 per 1,000, even plain text pages that have no tables. Those only need Read at $1.50.

A cost that grows faster than your number of questions is another clue. It often means the agent is searching more per question over time.

**Quickest check**

Pull a sample of recent traces. Count the tool calls per question, and average them. Multiply your monthly questions by that average, then by the price, and divide by 1,000. If that number is far above your estimate, your "uses per question" figure was wrong.

learn:stops.a:
The simple sum, uses times price divided by 1,000, is a good start. Here are three places where it needs extra care.

**Agents that vary a lot per question.** An average of "2 searches per question" can hide a few questions that trigger 20 searches, or an agent stuck in a loop. Look at the spread in your traces, not just the average. Plan for the high end, and cap searches per task so one bad question can't blow the budget.

**Prices that aren't flat.** Real price lists often have tiers (cheaper after a certain volume), free monthly allowances, or prices that change. Check the provider's current pricing page. If there are tiers, work out the cost for each tier separately and add them up.

**Hidden extra uses.** Retries after an error are usually billed as new calls. Search results get fed to the model, so you pay for those tokens too. Documents that get updated must be read again, so count each new version, not just each document. Add these to your count before you multiply.

judge.notes: Tiers, free allowances and retries billed as new calls are not in the lesson, but they do not contradict it and are reasonable extra care.

learn:term.a:
Most cost planning for AI looks at tokens. Tokens are the small chunks of text a model reads and writes, and model bills are based on them. But some tools don't charge by tokens. They charge **each time you use them**, or **for each page** they read. If you only count tokens, you miss part of the bill.

Here is how that goes wrong. A team builds the HR assistant. They budget for the model's tokens and assume one web search per question. That would be 30,000 searches at $14 per 1,000, so $420 a month.

Then they look at the traces. Traces are the logs of every step the agent took. The agent actually searches **3 times** per question. That's 90,000 searches, so $1,260 a month. That's three times what they planned, and it's just for search.

Documents can do the same thing. Say the agent re-reads the same pages for every question, using the $10 Layout service. You pay again on every question, when reading once at $1.50 might have been enough.

So the habit that matters is simple. Count the uses, multiply by the price, and divide by 1,000. Then find the cheapest way to do the work, and do it once.

*The idea.* "So I work out the monthly net first: saving per task times tasks a month, minus fixed costs. I only divide the build cost by it if the net is above zero. If it isn't, payback is `None`, Python's word for no value. That means the build never pays for itself."

"Why return `None` instead of zero, or a very large number?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Zero would claim the build pays back instantly. A very large number still suggests it pays back someday. `None` says plainly that there is no payback. It also forces whoever uses the result to deal with that case on purpose.

**Warning signs in the numbers**

- **The code crashes on division.** The net came out exactly zero, and you can't divide by zero.
- **Payback is huge, like 400 months.** The net is positive but tiny. Running costs eat almost all the savings. That is a real result, not a bug, but it's a warning.
- **Break-even is a fraction**, like `408.2`. It should be rounded up to a whole task.

**Warning signs in real use**

- **The saving per task looked great, then the budget didn't shrink.** Someone counted soft savings (quieter afternoons) instead of hard savings (fewer hires, less overtime). Or they left out the cost of mistakes nobody caught.
- **Real volume falls short of the guess.** The POC (proof of concept, the small trial) measures far fewer tasks a month than planned.

**Quickest check**

Put the measured tasks a month next to break-even. If measured is close to or below break-even, the plan is in trouble. Then swap each guess logged in MLflow for the number the POC measured, and recompute.

Here are three places where the simple formulas need extra care.

**The saving per task is zero or negative.** If the AI costs more per task than doing it by hand, or uncaught mistakes eat the whole saving, break-even makes no sense. You can't divide by zero, and a negative answer means no task count will ever cover costs. Check that the saving is above zero first, and treat "never pays back" as a real answer.

**The system gets much bigger.** Fixed costs are not fixed forever. At ten times the volume you may need more hosting or more monitoring, so costs jump in steps. Rework the plan at each size you expect, not just today's.

learn:term.q: How is “hard saving” different from “soft saving”?
learn:term.a:
A **hard saving** is saved time that turns into real money you no longer spend. The lesson gives two examples: fewer new hires, or less overtime. A **soft saving** is saved time that doesn't change what you pay. Staff get quieter afternoons, but the payroll stays the same.

An everyday comparison: you start cooking at home. Cancelling a meal-delivery subscription is a hard saving, because less money leaves your account each month. Simply feeling less rushed at dinnertime is soft. It's nice, but your bank balance doesn't move.

Here is how they fit together. Only hard savings count in the **saving per task** number. That's why the owner must confirm the saved staff time is real money before you use it. Soft savings stay out of the maths.

In the HR example, the saving is about $5.64 a ticket. That is $8 today, minus about $1.87 with AI, minus 50 cents for mistakes nobody caught. The 2.3-month payback only holds if that saving is hard. If part of it is only soft, the real monthly net is smaller, and payback takes longer.

**The counting is the other way round.** The limit counts what a request *asks for*: the prompt plus the longest answer you allow (`max_tokens`). So each request counts as *more* than its output, not less. If only output tokens counted, you would hit the limit less often, not more.

**It doesn't explain "every morning".** A counting rule applies all day. It can't make errors appear only at one time. The clue in the question is timing. The average is fine, but errors cluster in the morning. That points to a rush, when many requests land in the same few minutes.
