The fix is to plan for that rush, the same way a café adds staff for lunch.

"It was sized from the daily average, not the busiest minute" is better because it names the real cause: an unchanged limit meeting uneven traffic.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'cost is about your bill' line and the 'many people open HR tickets at the start of the day' detail go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:1:0.a:
The daily token total is a real number, and it is close to where your sizing starts. The lesson begins with tasks a day, and multiplying by tokens per task gives you that total.

But it doesn't answer this question. Neither limit in the lesson counts tokens a day. Both count per minute. The Foundry deployment's quota is in tokens per minute (TPM). The gateway's rate limits are per minute too. A daily total spreads your traffic evenly across the day, and that hides the busiest minute. That is exactly the mistake the lesson warns about. Sizing from the average leads to error 429, "too many requests."

You have also already used the daily figure. You turned tasks a day into tokens in the busiest minute. Checking the daily total again adds nothing new.

What's still unchecked is the second limit on the path. Every request passes through the gateway, the front door, before it reaches the model. The gateway has its own per-minute limits.

"The gateway's rate limits too" is better because the gateway can also send back error 429, even when the model's quota has room to spare.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Nothing: that's the only limit”?
check:1:2.a:
"Nothing: that's the only limit" gets one thing right. The Foundry deployment's quota is a real limit, and checking your busiest minute against it is the correct first step. If your number fits, that part of the path is safe.

What it misses is that the deployment is not the only place a request can be stopped. Every request reaches the model through the gateway. The gateway is a front door that all traffic passes through. It has its own rate limits, which are caps on how much it lets through each minute. These are set separately from the model's quota, often by the platform team.

So your traffic can fit the deployment's quota and still be turned away at the gateway. Users would see the same error 429, "too many requests". From their side, it does not matter which limit said no.

"The gateway's rate limits too" is better because it checks every limit on the path, and any one of them can send back a 429.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Each task is sent three times”?
check:2:0.a:
"Each task is sent three times" gets one thing right. Multiplying by 3 does raise your token count, just as sending every task three times would. So the arithmetic looks the same.

But the reason is wrong. Nothing gets sent twice. Each task still arrives once and asks for its tokens once. The burst factor is not about repeats or retries.

It is about timing. When you divide the busiest hour by 60, you get the average minute of that hour. That assumes tasks arrive evenly, one steady trickle. They don't. Some minutes in that hour get a cluster of tasks, and others get almost none. The limit is checked minute by minute, so a single crowded minute can go over the tokens-per-minute limit and cause error 429, even if the hour as a whole fits.

The burst factor covers that gap. A burst factor of 3 means "the busiest minute is about three times busier than the average minute of that hour."

"Some minutes are far busier than others" is the better answer because it names the real cause: tasks bunch up unevenly within the hour, so you size for the crowded minute, not the average one.

check:2:1.q: Why not “To leave room for three models”?
check:2:1.a:
"To leave room for three models" gets one thing right. Leaving some spare room above your estimate is a good habit. The lesson even says to ask for a limit above your number.

But the 3 has nothing to do with how many models you run. Each **deployment** (one copy of a model, set up for you) has its own **quota**, its own tokens-per-minute limit. You don't multiply by the number of models to size one of them.

The burst factor is about time, not models. Your busy-hour figure is an average across 60 minutes. Real traffic is lumpy. Inside that hour, some minutes get a pile of requests and others get almost none. The burst factor says how much busier the busiest minute is than an average minute of that hour. 3 is just a fair first guess until the POC measures the real 1-minute peaks.

If you skip it, that lumpy minute goes over the limit, and users get error 429, "too many requests."

"Some minutes are far busier than others" is the better answer because it names the real reason: traffic bunches up within the hour, and you must size for that peak minute.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Size for the busiest minute, not the day” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Limits are checked minute by minute, not across the whole day. A day that looks calm on average can still break in one busy minute.

Some quick terms. Your app talks to a **deployment**: one copy of a model, set up for you on Azure AI Foundry. Each deployment has a **quota**, the most it may use. It is counted in **tokens per minute**, or TPM. Requests also pass through a **gateway**, a front door with its own per-minute limits.

Now an example. An HR bot gets 270 tickets a day. Each ticket asks for 25,000 tokens, which is the prompt plus the longest answer allowed. Spread over an 8-hour day, that is about 14,000 tokens a minute. That looks fine against a 20,000 TPM quota.

But a fifth of the tickets arrive in the busiest hour. The busiest minute is about 3 times that hour's average. That comes to about 67,500 tokens in one minute.

That minute goes over the quota. Users get error 429, "too many requests", right when most people need the bot.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Daily count to busiest minute” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* Traffic is never even. If I size from the daily average, the busiest minute goes over the model's tokens-per-minute limit. Users then get error 429, "too many requests".

*The idea.* So I size for the busiest minute. I start with tasks a day. I keep the share that arrives in the busiest hour and turn that into tasks a minute. Then I multiply by a burst factor, which says how much busier the peak minute is than an average minute in that hour. Three is a fair first guess. Then I multiply by the tokens each task asks for. Last, I check the result against two limits: the deployment's quota (the most it may use) and the gateway's rate limits. The gateway is the front door every request passes through.

*The edge case.* I count tokens asked for, not tokens used. That means the prompt plus the longest answer I allow, because that's what the quota counts.

**Likely follow-up:** "Where do your numbers come from?"

*Hint:* The owner gives tasks a day. The POC measures the busy hour, the burst, and tokens per task. The platform team gives both limits.

judge.notes: No clear problems; the only minor weakness is that 'POC' is never explained, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

The clearest sign is error 429, "too many requests", that comes in clumps. It shows up at certain times, like Monday morning or just after lunch. The rest of the day is quiet.

Your usage chart looks fine because it shows hourly or daily averages, well under the quota. The average hides the spikes.

A test that sends requests at a steady pace often passes. Then real users arrive in bursts and it fails.

You may also see 429s even when your busiest minutes look under the limit. That usually means you counted tokens **used**, not tokens **asked for**. Remember the prompt plus `max_tokens`, the longest answer you allow.

Sometimes the model's quota has room, but users still get 429. Then the gateway's rate limit, the front door's own cap, is the one being hit.

**Quickest check**

Pull the busiest minutes from the gateway's usage table. Then line up the times of the 429 errors in your logs against them. If they match, you sized for the average. Next, compare that peak, plus room for `max_tokens`, against both the deployment quota and the gateway limit.

judge.notes: Minor overreach: "If they match, you sized for the average" is stronger than the lesson supports, since matching peaks could also point to the max_tokens miscount or the gateway limit; otherwise acceptable.

learn:stops.a:
The rule holds up well, but here are three places it needs extra care.

**Agents that loop.** An agent may call the model several times for one task, and the number of calls changes from task to task. A single "tokens per task" figure then hides the big ones. Measure many tasks, size from the heavy end rather than the middle, and cap how many steps an agent may take.

**Traffic that changes over time.** Your burst factor and busy-hour share come from one week of a pilot. A launch day, month-end rush, or more users will change them. Re-run the busiest-minutes check on the gateway's usage table often, keep headroom (spare room above your number), and set an alert before you reach the limit.

**Limits shared with other apps.** The deployment quota or gateway limit may be shared by other teams. Your busiest minute adds to theirs, and they may peak at the same time. Ask the platform team whether the limit is shared. If it is, plan with their numbers included, or ask for your own deployment.

judge.notes: The answer is acceptable. Minor nits: the shared-limits paragraph runs to four sentences, and 'one week of a pilot' is an assumption the lesson does not state.

learn:term.a:
**Size** is the decision itself: how many tokens a minute your system must handle. It is a single number you land on.

**Capacity planning** is the habit of making that decision *ahead of time*, before real users arrive. It covers the whole job: gathering the inputs, working out the busiest minute, and checking the result against the limits.

So size is the *what*, and capacity planning is the *when and how*. You size a system as part of capacity planning.

**An everyday comparison:** a café owner decides they need four staff for the lunch rush. That number is the size. Writing the staff rota a week before, using last month's busy days, is capacity planning. Deciding on the spot at 12:30, when the queue is out the door, is too late.

**In the lesson's example,** capacity planning means:

- taking 270 HR tickets a day from the owner
- using the busy-hour share, burst and tokens per ticket from the POC (the trial version of the project)
- checking against the quota and gateway limits from the platform team

The size it lands on is 75,000 tokens a minute. You then ask for a limit above that, before launch.

judge.notes: No major problems. It is near the word limit, and "before launch" and the POC gloss go slightly beyond the lesson's text.

check:0:1.a:
Your math is right. 42,000 divided by 3,000 really is 14. So "14" is exactly how much capacity your busiest minute needs.

The catch is that the deployment won't accept 14. A deployment is the copy of the model you set up and pay for. For `gpt-4.1` on Global, the smallest deployment you can create is 15 PTUs. A PTU (provisioned throughput unit) is one block of model capacity kept just for you. You can't order fewer than the minimum, even if your app would never use the extra one.

Think of buying eggs by the box. You might need 14 eggs, but if the smallest box holds 15, you walk out with 15. Capacity is sold in whole blocks, not in any amount you like.

That extra PTU isn't wasted, either. It gives you a little headroom, meaning spare room, so a minute slightly busier than you expected still fits.

"15" is better because it is the smallest amount you can actually buy that still covers your busiest minute.

check:0:2.a:
"42" starts from the right number. 42,000 tokens a minute is the correct busiest-minute load, with output already weighted. But "42" just drops the thousands. It never divides by what one PTU handles.

A PTU (provisioned throughput unit) is one block of model capacity kept just for you. Here each one handles 3,000 tokens a minute. So the real sum is 42,000 divided by 3,000, which gives 14 PTUs, not 42.

Then there's one more step. A deployment has a minimum size. For `gpt-4.1` on Global, that's 15 PTUs. 14 is under the minimum, so you round up to 15. It's like eggs sold in boxes: you can't buy 14 if the smallest box holds 15.

Buying 42 would also be costly. Reserved monthly, that's 42 × $260 = $10,920. The right size costs 15 × $260 = $3,900. You'd pay nearly three times as much for capacity you never use.

"15" is better because it divides the load by one PTU's capacity, then rounds up to the deployment's minimum.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Nothing, because it was idle”?
check:1:1.a:
"Nothing, because it was idle" mixes up the two ways to pay.

**What it gets right:** that is exactly how pay per token works. With the Standard option, you pay for each token (a small chunk of text) the model reads or writes. No requests all weekend means no tokens, so no bill.

**What it misses:** a PTU (provisioned throughput unit) works differently. You are renting a block of model capacity that is kept just for you. That capacity sits ready every hour, so you pay for every hour, whether you use it or not. The lesson also notes that billing can't be paused. It runs until you delete the deployment. Reserved monthly terms are billed in full too.

For example, 15 PTUs on Global at $1.00 an hour, idle for a 48-hour weekend, still costs 15 × $1.00 × 48 = $720.

Think of it like renting a parking space. You pay for the space even when your car isn't in it.

"The full hourly price" is better because PTUs charge for capacity that is held for you, not for the work you actually do.

check:1:2.a:
"Half the hourly price" gets one thing right. You do still pay something over the weekend, even though nothing is running. So it avoids the trap of thinking idle hours are free.

But it assumes the price drops when the deployment (your set-up copy of the model) sits idle. That isn't how a PTU works.

A PTU is capacity kept just for you. Nobody else can use it, whether you send a request or not. So you are paying for the reservation itself, not for the work done. Busy hour, quiet hour, or empty weekend, each hour costs the same.

The lesson also says billing can't be paused. It keeps running until you delete the deployment. There is no "idle rate" and no half-price mode.

This is the real difference from pay per token. With pay per token, an empty weekend costs nothing, because you only pay for tokens (small chunks of text) used.

"The full hourly price" is better because a PTU charges every hour for capacity held for you, used or not, until the deployment is deleted.

check:2:1.a:
"They fail with error 429" describes what happens **without** spillover. That part is real. Error 429 means "too many requests." The service is saying it has no room for you right now. A full PTU deployment with nothing behind it will send that error back.

But the question says spillover is **on**. Spillover exists to stop exactly that failure. When your reserved capacity is full, spillover sends the extra requests somewhere else instead of turning them away.

That "somewhere else" is a pay-per-token deployment. It is the Standard kind, where you pay for each token used. So the extra requests still get answered. You pay for them by the token, on top of your hourly PTU bill.

So the 429 answer misses the whole point of the setting. It treats spillover as if it did nothing.

"They go to a pay-per-token deployment" is better because it describes what spillover actually does: it moves the overflow to Standard capacity, so the requests are served instead of failing.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that a full PTU deployment returns 429 isn't stated in the lesson, but it fits the lesson's 'instead of failing' and is true.

check:2:2.q: Why not “They wait for the next hour”?
check:2:2.a:
It's an easy mix-up, because the lesson does mention hours. A PTU deployment is billed by the hour. That part is true. But billing is about how you pay. It doesn't control what happens to your requests.

Here's what the answer misses. Capacity is sized per minute, from the busiest minute. When that minute's capacity is full, nothing in the setup holds extra requests for an hour. A user waiting an hour for a reply would be a broken app anyway.

**Spillover** exists for exactly this moment. It's a setting that sends the extra requests somewhere else when the PTU deployment is full. That somewhere is a pay-per-token deployment, which is a second deployment that charges for each token used. So the request still gets answered right away. You just pay for its tokens at the normal per-token price, instead of the request failing.

"They go to a pay-per-token deployment" is better because that is exactly what spillover does: it moves the overflow to pay-per-token so the extra requests are served now, not delayed or dropped.

judge.notes: No significant problems. Minor: 'right away' and 'normal per-token price' go slightly beyond the lesson's wording, and 'PTU' is not re-explained.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Normalize, divide, then round up to the minimum…” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem.* With pay per token, a busy minute can hit error 429, meaning "too many requests." A PTU (provisioned throughput unit) is model capacity kept just for you. The question is how many to buy.

*The idea.* Size from the busiest minute. First, normalize: convert everything into input tokens. For gpt-4.1, one output token counts as 4 input tokens. So 30,000 input plus 3,000 output becomes 42,000. Next, divide by what one PTU handles, which is 3,000 a minute. That gives 14.

*The edge case.* Capacity is sold in whole blocks. On Global, gpt-4.1 needs at least 15 PTUs, then steps of 5. So 14 becomes 15. It's like eggs: the smallest box holds 15.

**A likely follow-up**

"Will PTUs save us money?"

Hint: say no. They buy capacity, not savings. For a load this busy all month, pay per token is about $3,679. Reserved PTUs cost $3,900, and hourly PTUs cost $10,950. What you pay for is steady speed. Then mention spillover. If the PTU deployment is full, extra requests go to pay per token instead of failing.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that the PTU sizing went wrong**

A **PTU** (provisioned throughput unit) is a block of model capacity kept just for you. Here is what a slip looks like in your numbers.

- **The count is suspiciously low.** Output tokens were counted the same as input tokens. Or the size came from an average minute instead of the busiest one.
- **The count isn't a size you can buy.** It has a fraction, like 14.3. It sits below the deployment's minimum. Or it falls between steps, like 17 on Global or 60 on Regional.
- **The budget expected savings.** Someone thought PTUs would cost less than pay per token. The lesson's example shows they cost about the same or more, even when busy all month.
- **The bill keeps running.** Someone assumed a deployment could be paused. It can't. Billing runs until it is deleted.
- **Requests fail when the PTU deployment is full.** **Spillover** was left off. Spillover sends extra requests to a pay-per-token deployment instead.

**Quickest check:** Run the lesson's worked example (30,000 input, 3,000 output) through your sizing. You should get 42,000 normalized tokens and 15 PTUs. If you get anything else, look again at the busiest-minute numbers and the rounding.

learn:stops.a:
**When does PTU sizing stop working?**

**1. Traffic that spikes rarely.** You size from the busiest minute, so a short daily spike means paying for idle capacity all the other hours. Billing can't be paused, so this gets expensive. Stay on pay-per-token, or buy a small PTU base and let spillover send the extra requests to pay-per-token.

**2. A different model or deployment type.** The output weight, the tokens one PTU handles, the minimum and the step size all change. For `gpt-4.1`, "minimum 15, then steps of 5" holds only on Global or Data Zone, while Regional starts at 50 and goes up in steps of 50. Look up the numbers for your exact model and deployment type before you divide and round.

**3. Usage that changes over time.** Agents often add tool calls and longer answers, so output tokens grow and each one counts several times. Last month's busiest minute can quietly become too small. Measure the busiest minute again regularly and resize, and delete deployments you no longer use.

learn:term.a:
Think of a restaurant where you've booked a private room. Your table is always waiting. If more friends show up than the room holds, the host seats them in the main dining room instead of sending them home. They still eat. They just order from the regular menu at regular prices.

Spillover works the same way. Your PTU deployment is the private room: capacity kept just for you. A "deployment" means a model set up and ready to answer requests. When the PTU deployment is full, extra requests go to a pay-per-token deployment. They get answered instead of failing. You pay per token only for that overflow.

In the lesson's example, the busiest minute comes to 42,000 tokens once each output token is counted as 4 input tokens. Divided by 3,000 per PTU, that gives 14. That's under the minimum, so you buy 15.

Now suppose a minute ever runs busier than those 15 PTUs can handle. Spillover sends the extra requests to pay per token. You get steady, reserved capacity for normal load, plus a safety net for surprise spikes.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Output tokens cost less than input tokens, per …”?
check:0:1.a:
That option fails in two ways.

First, it is usually not even true. On most price lists, output tokens (the words the model writes) cost *more* per token than input tokens (the words you send in), not less.

Second, even if it were true, it would not explain the mistake. The teammate's error is about *how many* tokens get used, not what each token costs. Pricing per token only matters after you have the right count. And their count is wrong.

Here is why. On step 1 the agent sends the first context. On step 2 it sends that again, plus step 1's answer and tool result. Each later step resends everything before it, so each input is bigger than the last. Six steps cost far more than six copies of the first call. It is like an email thread where every reply quotes everything above it.

"Each step resends everything that earlier steps added" is better because it names the real cause: the input grows every step, so the teammate's count was too low.

judge.notes: The claim that output tokens usually cost more than input tokens is not in the lesson, but it is true in practice and does not contradict the lesson, so I let it pass.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The first call is always the most expensive step”?
check:0:2.a:
That option points the wrong way. The first call is actually the *cheapest* step, not the most expensive.

Here is why. On the first call, the context is only the instructions and the question. The context is everything the agent sends to the model. After that call, the model's answer and any tool result get added to the context. On the next call, the agent sends all of it again, plus the new parts. So each call reads more input tokens than the one before.

In the lesson's example, the calls read 4000, then 5000, then 6000 tokens. The first call is the smallest one.

The option does get one thing right. It notices that the calls don't all cost the same. But it guesses the wrong direction. If the first call really were the biggest, "6 times the first call" would be too high. In fact it is too low, because every later step costs more than the first.

"Each step resends everything that earlier steps added" is better because it names the real mistake: the input keeps growing, so six steps cost more than six first calls.

judge.notes: No significant problems; it is near the length limit, and 'cheapest' refers to input tokens, which matches the lesson's example.

check:1:1.q: Why not “That one call, times the price list”?
check:1:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. The price list really is how you turn tokens into dollars. That part stays.

What it misses is that an agent doesn't make one call per task. It makes many. On every step it resends the whole **context**, meaning the instructions, the question, and every earlier answer and tool result. So each call is bigger than the one before. In the lesson's example, three steps read 4000, then 5000, then 6000 tokens. That adds up to 15000, not 4000.

One test call can't show you that growth. It also can't show spread. Hard tasks take more steps, so some runs cost far more than others. In the research system, a team of agents used about 15 times the tokens of a plain chat. Pricing from one call would miss most of the bill.

The right answer is "Whole runs on real tasks, from traces." A **trace** is the record of each step an agent took, including its token counts. It's better because it measures what a full task actually costs, and it gives you a low, typical and high count to price from.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only loose spots are 'not 4000' (the lesson contrasts 15000 with 12000) and 'miss most of the bill', which stretches the 15x team figure.

check:1:2.q: Why not “A plain chat with the same model”?
check:1:2.a:
A plain chat gets one thing right. It uses the same model, so the price per token is the same. That part of your sum would be correct.

What it misses is how an agent actually works. A plain chat is roughly one question and one answer. An agent loops. On every step it resends the whole **context**: the instructions, the question, every earlier answer and every tool result. So the input gets bigger each step, and a plain chat never shows that growth.

The lesson's numbers show how big the gap is. One agent used about 4 times the tokens of a plain chat. A team of agents used about 15 times. If you priced from a plain chat, your estimate could be several times too low.

A plain chat also gives you only one number. Hard tasks take more steps, so you need a low, typical and high count.

"Whole runs on real tasks, from traces" is better because **traces** (the step-by-step records your POC saves) capture every step's tokens on real work, including the growing context and the spread from easy tasks to hard ones.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Only the easy count, the usual case”?
check:2:0.a:
"Only the easy count" gets one thing right. It uses a real number, measured from real tasks in the POC (your trial build). And if easy tasks really are common, that number does describe many runs.

But it hides the expensive end. Hard tasks took 12 steps, not 3. On every step the agent resends the whole context (everything so far). So each extra step costs more than the one before. A 12-step task costs much more than four times a 3-step task.

If you report only the easy count, your budget looks small and safe. Then the hard tasks arrive and the real bill is far higher. Also, nothing in the question says easy tasks are the usual case. Calling them "usual" is a guess.

Pricing should cover the whole spread of real runs, not the cheapest slice.

"A low, a typical and a high count" is the right answer. It shows the cheap case, the normal case and the worst case, so the price you plan for matches what hard tasks will actually cost.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Only the hardest, to be safe”?
check:2:2.a:
"Only the hardest, to be safe" gets one thing right. Hard tasks really do cost more. A 12-step run resends a much bigger context each step than a 3-step run, so its token count is far higher. Knowing that worst case helps you set a ceiling on spending.

But reporting only that number misleads people. Most of the 20 tasks may have been easy. If you price every task as if it took 12 steps, your estimate could be several times too high. A budget that inflated can make a good project look too expensive to build.

It also hides the spread. The people reading your report can't tell whether hard tasks happen once in a while or all the time. That mix is what decides the real monthly bill.

And "the hardest" is only the hardest of 20. Real users may send something harder still, so this number isn't truly "safe" either.

A low, a typical and a high count is the better answer, because it shows the usual cost and the full range together, so people can plan for the normal case and still prepare for the expensive one.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Price the whole run, not one call” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
When you test an agent, it's tempting to send one request, note its token count, and multiply by the number of tasks you expect. That estimate is always too low.

An agent works in steps. On each step it resends the whole **context**: the instructions, the question, and every earlier answer and tool result. So each step reads more than the one before.

A small example: the first call reads 4,000 tokens. Price from that, and you plan for 4,000 per task. But a three-step run reads 4,000, then 5,000, then 6,000. That's 15,000 tokens, nearly four times your plan. Hard tasks take more steps, so they cost even more.

In real work, the budget runs out early. Someone gets a surprise bill. A product that looked cheap can turn out to lose money on every user.

So price from whole runs. An **MLflow trace** is a step-by-step record of one run, and it adds up the tokens of every call for you. Measure several real tasks, then give a low, typical and high count.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'always too low' claim is a little strong, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “A running total that grows” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* An agent doesn't send only the new bit on each step. It resends the whole context: the instructions, the question, every earlier answer and every tool result. So the price of one call badly underestimates the price of a task. (A token is a small chunk of text. Models count and charge by tokens.)

*The idea.* Picture an email thread where every reply quotes everything above it. Each step reads the full thread, then the thread grows. Start at 4,000 tokens and run three steps: the agent reads 4,000, then 5,000, then 6,000. That's 15,000 in, not 12,000.

*The edge case.* Hard tasks take more steps, and each extra step costs more than the last. So I measure whole runs from traces on real tasks and give low, typical and high counts. I also set `recursion_limit` so a stuck agent can't loop up a huge bill.

**Likely follow-up**

"How would you cut that cost?"

Hint: shrink what gets resent. Summarise old tool results, keep only recent messages, and cap the step count. Then name the trade-off: dropping context can make the agent forget something it needs.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The bill beats the estimate.** Your budget said one amount. The real invoice is several times higher. That usually means someone priced one call and multiplied by the number of steps.
- **Every step looks the same size.** In your numbers, each step's input is the same. In a real agent, each step's input should be bigger than the last, because it carries everything before it.
- **The estimate is one number.** There is no low, typical and high. Hard tasks take more steps, and each extra step costs more than the one before. So a single number hides the expensive runs.
- **Long runs surprise you.** Some tasks hit the `recursion_limit` (the cap on how many steps a run may take). Those runs cost far more than your "typical" figure.

**The quickest check**

Open one trace (the step-by-step record of a run) from a real task. Look at the input tokens for each step. They should climb, like 4000, then 5000, then 6000. Add them up. If that total is clearly bigger than your estimate for the run, the estimate skipped the growth.

learn:stops.a:
The simple "resend everything" sum is a good starting model. Here are three places where real runs behave differently.

**1. Prompt caching.** Some model providers store the start of a prompt they have already seen. They then charge less for those repeated tokens. Your token count still grows each step, but the dollar cost grows more slowly. Check the price list for a separate "cached input" price, and read cached tokens from your traces.

**2. Long runs hit the context window.** The context window is the most text a model can read at once. Long agent runs often trim old messages or swap them for a short summary. So the context stops growing in a straight line. Measure real traces instead of trusting the simple sum.

**3. Teams of agents.** In a multi-agent system, each helper agent usually starts with its own fresh, smaller context. That means there is not one single growing thread. Add up each agent's whole run separately, then combine them. This is how a team can reach about 15 times the tokens of a plain chat.

judge.notes: Passes. Minor: items 1 and 3 run to four sentences against the two-to-three limit, and the claim that separate agent runs explain the 15x figure is plausible but not stated in the lesson.

learn:term.a:
An **agent** is a program that uses an AI model to finish a task in several steps, not just one reply.

Think of an assistant handling a request. They think, look something up, read what they found, then decide what to do next. They repeat this until the job is done. The twist: the model remembers nothing between calls. So every time the assistant asks it something, they hand over the whole folder so far.

Each round is one **step**. In a step the model writes something, often a request to use a **tool**. A tool is a helper the agent can call, like a search or a database lookup. The tool's reply then gets added to the folder.

In the lesson's example, each pair in `steps` is one agent step:

- `out` is what the model wrote in that step.
- `tool` is what the tool sent back.
- The last step, `[500, 0]`, is the final answer. No tool is used, so its tool result is `0`.

In the LangChain snippet, `graph` is the agent itself. `recursion_limit` caps how many steps it may take.

judge.notes: Minor: the claim that [500, 0] is the final answer with no tool is an inference the lesson never states, but it fits the example.

check:0:0.q: Why not “A model that is half the price per token”?
check:0:0.a:
Halving the price per token sounds like a big cut. It does lower a real cost, and the model is the line people usually think of first. But in this assistant, the model is one of the smallest lines.

The model costs $390 a month. Half price saves $195 a month. Over 24 months that is $4,680. That is about 1% of the $396,760 total.

What it misses is where the money actually goes. The biggest single item is people checking and redoing answers: $10,800 a month, or $259,200 over two years. That is more than 25 times the whole model cost for the same period.

So even a small win there beats the cheaper model. Cutting the checking work by just 5% saves $540 a month. That is already more than the $195 the half-price model would save.

This is the lesson's main point. The tokens are often the smallest part of the total cost of ownership (TCO), so look at the biggest item first.

"Fewer answers for a person to check or redo" is better because it shrinks the largest line in the budget, where every saving counts most.

check:0:2.q: Why not “A cheaper security review before launch”?
check:0:2.a:
A cheaper security review does lower the cost, so it isn't wrong. But it is a one-off build cost: you pay it once, before launch. In the HR assistant it was $5,000 out of $396,760. That's only about 1% of the total. Even halving it would save just $2,500.

What it misses is where most of the money goes. The biggest item is people checking and redoing answers, at $10,800 a month. That monthly figure stays the same, but you pay it every month for 24 months. So the total for that line builds up to $259,200. That's about two thirds of everything the system costs over two years.

The lesson's advice is to look at the biggest single item first, because that is where a saving matters most.

"Fewer answers for a person to check or redo" is better because it shrinks the largest line, a cost paid all 24 months. Even a 10% cut there saves $25,920, about five times the whole security review.

check:1:0.a:
"Tokens for each question" is a real cost, so you were right to think of it. It just isn't paid once.

A token is a small chunk of text, often part of a word. The model charges for every token it reads and writes. Each time someone asks the assistant a question, it embeds the question (turns it into numbers so it can be searched) and writes an answer. Both use tokens.

Questions keep arriving every day the system is live. So this cost comes back every month and grows with how many questions people ask. In the lesson's groups, that puts it under **Run**, not **Build**.

The trap is the word "each." It can sound like a single event. But "each question" really means "every question, for the whole life of the system."

"Indexing all the documents at first" is better because you chunk and embed the whole document collection one time, before launch. After that, only new documents cost anything, so the first big indexing run is a true one-off.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the claim 'before launch' and 'only new documents cost anything' go slightly beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:1:2.a:
"Searching the vector index" is a real cost of a RAG assistant, so it belongs on your list. It just sits in the wrong group.

A **vector index** is the store of document passages, each turned into a list of numbers (an embedding) so the system can find passages with similar meaning. **Searching** it means looking up the best passages for a question.

That search happens every time a user asks something. More questions mean more searches. The search service, such as Azure AI Search or Databricks AI Search, also keeps running and billing you whether it is busy or not. So this cost comes back every month for the whole life of the system. In the lesson's groups, it is a **Run** cost, not a **Build** cost.

The option may feel one-off because the index sounds like something you set up once. But setting it up and searching it are different steps.

"Indexing all the documents at first" is better because it happens only once, when you first chunk and embed the whole document collection, and it is never repeated in full.

check:2:0.a:
It's an easy mix-up, because evals do appear in the **Build** group. Building the eval set is a Build cost. An eval set is the collection of test questions and good answers you use to score the system. You make it once, before launch, and pay for it once.

But the question is about **re-running** those evals. That doesn't happen once. It happens every time the model or the prompt changes, for as long as the system is live. Models get updated by the provider. Prompts get tweaked when answers drift. Each change means someone runs the tests again and checks the results.

So "Build, paid once" gets the subject right (evals) but the timing wrong. It treats a repeating cost as a one-off. That matters for the total, because a repeating cost gets multiplied by every month you run the system. In the HR example, evals cost 1100 a month, which adds up to 26400 over two years.

"Maintain, keeping it working" is better because re-running evals is ongoing work you keep paying for to keep the system trustworthy after it's built.

check:2:1.a:
"Run, paid every month" gets one thing right. Re-running evals does cost money again and again, not just once. In the HR assistant example, `evals` sits in the `monthly` list next to `model` and `hosting`. So in the final total, it adds up the same way.

What it misses is *why* the cost happens. Run costs come from using the system. Each question from a user spends tokens, hosting time and search. More traffic means a bigger bill.

Re-running evals has a different cause. An **eval** is a set of test questions with known good answers, used to check the system still answers well. You re-run it because something changed, like a new model version or a reworded prompt. It doesn't depend on how many people ask questions. It is upkeep, like servicing a car rather than buying fuel.

Keeping the groups apart helps when you look for savings. Fewer queries cut Run costs. Fewer changes, or cheaper checks, cut Maintain costs.

"Maintain, keeping it working" is better because this cost comes from changes to the system, not from people using it.

judge.notes: Minor: the claims that Run costs scale with traffic and that cuts split by group go slightly beyond the lesson (hosting is not strictly per-query), but nothing contradicts it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “One-off plus monthly times months” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* Teams often price an AI system by its token bill. But tokens are usually the smallest part. The real cost is everything it takes to own the system for its whole life.

*The idea.* Total cost of ownership is the one-off build costs, plus every monthly cost times the months you run it. Build costs include people's time, the eval set (a fixed set of test questions) and the security review. Monthly costs include tokens, hosting, monitoring and people checking answers. Then I look at the biggest single item, because that is where a saving matters most.

*A trade-off.* Monthly costs add up quietly. In one HR assistant example, people checking answers cost more than three times the whole build over two years. So a pricier model that cuts rework can be cheaper overall.

**A likely follow-up**

"What if usage grows over time?"

*Hint:* Say a flat monthly figure is only a starting estimate. Name the cost drivers that scale, like how many queries arrive and how much data you index. Then re-estimate each year as those change.

judge.notes: Minor: it says tokens are 'usually' the smallest part where the lesson says 'often', and the pricier-model point is an inference, not something the lesson states.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that TCO was skipped or done wrong**

- **The business case only counted tokens.** It looked cheap on paper. Then the real monthly spend came in several times higher. In the HR example the model is $390 a month, but the whole bill is $13,490.
- **Costs nobody planned for.** You see charges for the search index, the compute jobs that chunk (cut into passages) and embed documents, storage for traces, or staff time spent checking answers. None of them were in the estimate.
- **Savings aimed at the wrong place.** The team spends weeks switching to a cheaper model. Meanwhile people redoing answers cost far more every month.
- **The yearly total doesn't add up.** A common slip is forgetting to multiply monthly costs by 12 times the years. Another is multiplying one-off build costs by the months.

**Quickest check**

Put your estimate next to one real month's bill and the hours staff logged. Every real line should match a planned line. Then multiply each monthly line by the number of months and find the biggest one. If that item surprises you, the original estimate missed it.

learn:stops.a:
The simple rule (one-off costs, plus each monthly cost times the months) assumes the monthly costs stay flat. Here are three places where that needs care.

**Usage that grows.** A new assistant often starts small. Then more people use it and more documents get added. Tokens, search and compute climb month by month. Instead of one flat monthly number, estimate each year separately, or apply a growth rate, and add those up.

**Prices and models that change.** Token prices often drop, and providers retire old models. A forced model switch means re-running evals, re-tuning prompts, and maybe re-embedding every document. "Re-embedding" means turning all your text into number lists again. Treat this as a one-off cost you expect to repeat, say once a year.

**Shared platforms in bigger systems.** In a large company, one Databricks workspace or one on-call team may serve many apps. Charging the whole cost to one app makes it look too expensive. Split shared costs fairly, for example by each app's share of usage.

Also check that the biggest item can actually shrink. Some human review may be legally required.

learn:term.a:
**Maintain** means the work of keeping the system working well after it is built. It is a monthly cost, like **Run**, but it pays for upkeep rather than for answering questions.

Think of owning a bike. Buying it is the build cost. Riding it is the run cost. Pumping the tyres, oiling the chain and fixing a puncture is maintain. You don't do it to get anywhere. You do it so the bike keeps working.

For an AI system, maintain covers three things:

- **Re-running evals.** An eval set is a fixed list of test questions with known good answers. When the model or the prompt changes, you run them again to check nothing broke.
- **Updating prompts.** You adjust the instructions you give the model as needs change.
- **Someone on call.** A person is ready to fix problems when they happen.

In the HR assistant example, the maintain line is `"evals": 1100` inside `monthly`. That is $1,100 every month. Over 24 months it adds $26,400, which is more than three times the $8,000 one-off cost of building the eval set.

check:0:1.q: Why not “It grows by about 6 percent”?
check:0:1.a:
"It grows by about 6 percent" gets one thing right. The data itself did grow by about 6 percent. Going from 34 GB to 36 GB adds 2 GB, and 2 is about 6 percent of 34.

What it misses is how you are billed. A search service doesn't charge for each gigabyte you store. It charges for units, which are fixed blocks of capacity kept running every hour. You can only buy whole units, never part of one.

Here, one unit holds 35 GB. At 34 GB, everything fits in one unit. At 36 GB, you are 1 GB over, so you need a second unit. That second unit costs the same as the first, even though it is almost empty. So the bill goes from about $245 a month to about $490 a month.

Think of hotel rooms again. One extra guest past the room limit means booking a whole extra room, not paying a bit more for the same room.

"It doubles: you need a second unit" is better because the bill follows the number of whole units, and crossing 35 GB takes you from one unit to two.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing until you reach 70 GB”?
check:0:2.a:
"Nothing until you reach 70 GB" has a grain of truth. Two units hold 35 + 35 = 70 GB. So once you have two units, the bill stays flat all the way up to 70 GB. That part is right.

What it misses is *when* you get that second unit. One unit holds only 35 GB. At 34 GB you fit in one unit. At 36 GB you are 1 GB over, and you can't buy a "tiny bit" of a unit. You buy whole units only. So the second unit starts billing the moment you pass 35 GB, not at 70 GB.

Think of hotel rooms with 2 guests to a room. A third guest means booking a second room right away. You don't wait until a fourth guest arrives.

So 70 GB is where the *next* step happens, the jump from two units to three. The step this question asks about happens at 35 GB.

"It doubles: you need a second unit" is better because it puts the jump at the right place: passing 35 GB forces a second whole unit, so the bill goes from about $245 to about $490 a month.

check:1:1.a:
"It stays the same" gets one thing right. The number of chunks does not change. You still have 5 million of them. A "chunk" is one piece of text you turned into a vector.

What it misses is that each vector gets longer. A "dimension" is one number in the vector. Going from 1,536 to 3,072 dimensions means every chunk now stores twice as many numbers. Each number still takes 4 bytes.

The lesson's rule is: space = vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes. Only one of those three changed, and it doubled:

- 5,000,000 × 1,536 × 4 = 30,720,000,000 bytes, about 30.7 GB
- 5,000,000 × 3,072 × 4 = 61,440,000,000 bytes, about 61.4 GB

That matters for the bill, too. 30.7 GB fits in one 35 GB unit. 61.4 GB needs two.

"It doubles" is better because space grows in step with dimensions, so twice the numbers per vector means twice the bytes for the same chunks.

check:1:2.a:
"It halves" gets one thing right. The size does change by a factor of two, because 3,072 is exactly twice 1,536.

But it gets the direction backwards. Each vector is a list of numbers, and each number takes 4 bytes. The dimensions are how many numbers are in each vector. Going from 1,536 to 3,072 means each vector holds **more** numbers, not fewer. More numbers means more bytes.

The number of chunks stays the same: 5 million. So every one of those 5 million vectors gets twice as long. Here is the lesson's formula (vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes) for both cases:

- 5,000,000 × 1,536 × 4 = 30.72 GB
- 5,000,000 × 3,072 × 4 = 61.44 GB

Halving would only happen if you went the other way, from 3,072 down to 1,536. That is the "shorter vectors, smaller bill" idea from later in the lesson.

"It doubles" is better because space grows in step with the dimensions, so twice the numbers per vector means twice the bytes.

judge.notes: The arithmetic (30.72 GB and 61.44 GB) is right, it matches the lesson's formula, and it stays under 200 words. It only uses the lesson's simple size formula and does not give the search_units solution.

check:2:1.a:
"Nothing, because nobody searched" feels reasonable. Some cloud services do bill per use, like paying for each request. And it's true that no searches means no search work was done.

But Databricks AI Search doesn't bill that way. An **endpoint** is the running service that holds your vectors and answers searches. Once you create it, Databricks keeps machines switched on and ready for you, all day and all night. You pay for that reserved capacity, not for each search.

So the clock runs from the moment the endpoint exists. At the Standard rate of about `$0.28` an hour, a month of zero searches still costs about `$204`. Using it more doesn't raise that base cost, and leaving it idle doesn't lower it.

That's why idle endpoints are a common surprise on the bill. If you don't need one, delete it rather than leaving it sitting there.

"It still bills every hour it exists" is the better answer because it matches how the service charges: by the hours the capacity stays switched on, not by how many searches it gets.

judge.notes: Minor: the 'common surprise' and 'delete it' advice go slightly beyond the lesson, but nothing contradicts it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Only the space the vectors take”?
check:2:2.a:
That answer sounds sensible, because many cloud services do charge by storage. It gets one thing right: the size of your vectors matters. More gigabytes can mean you need more units.

But it misses how search services actually bill. You don't pay per gigabyte stored. You pay for capacity: whole units that sit running, ready to answer searches. A "unit" is a block of machine power and memory set aside just for you. An "endpoint" is the address your app sends searches to, backed by those units.

The meter runs on time, not on use or storage. A Databricks AI Search Standard unit costs about $0.28 an hour. That adds up to about $204 a month, whether anyone searches or not. Zero searches does not mean zero cost. It also doesn't shrink to "just the storage."

So an idle endpoint you forgot about still costs you the full unit price. If you don't need it, delete it.

"It still bills every hour it exists" is better because it names the real rule: you pay for each running unit by the hour, used or not.

judge.notes: The answer matches the lesson's $0.28 an hour and about $204 a month figures. Its definitions of 'unit' and 'endpoint' go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Work out the size, then round up to whole units” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* Vector search services don't bill by the gigabyte. They bill whole units of capacity that keep running every hour, used or not.

*The idea.* First I work out the size: number of vectors, times numbers per vector, times 4 bytes each. Two million chunks at 1,536 numbers is about 12.3 GB. Then I compare that to what one unit holds and round up, because you can't buy part of a unit. 73.7 GB on 35 GB units is 2.1, so I pay for 3.

*The trade-off.* The bill moves in steps. Growing from 34 GB to 36 GB doubles the cost. Shorter vectors can pull you back under a step. But quality may drop, so I'd test on an eval set first. An eval set is a fixed set of test questions with known good answers.

**A likely follow-up**

"Your data sits just over a unit boundary. What would you do?"

*Hint:* Give options, not one fix:
- Ask the model for fewer numbers per vector.
- Remove duplicate or outdated chunks.
- Accept the extra unit if quality matters more.

Also mention that an endpoint nobody searches still bills, so delete unused ones.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
Here are the warning signs that the sizing was skipped or done wrong.

**The bill is higher than your estimate.** Usually someone budgeted for gigabytes, not whole units. A small growth in chunks pushed the vectors past one unit, and the bill jumped a full step. For example, it went from one S1 unit (about $245 a month) to two.

**The estimate shows a fraction of a unit.** A plan that says "2.1 units" was never rounded up. You can only buy whole units, so the real bill is higher.

**You pay for an endpoint nobody uses.** An endpoint is the running search service you connect to. It still bills every hour it exists, even with zero searches.

**Answers got worse after shrinking vectors.** If someone cut the numbers per vector to save space, results may drop a little. Your eval set shows this. An eval set is your fixed list of test questions with known good answers.

**Quickest check:** run your estimate on the lesson's own examples. Try 34 GB, 36 GB and 73.7 GB against 35 GB units. You should get 1, 2 and 3 units. If any of those comes out different, your sizing is off.

learn:stops.a:
**When the simple size rule needs extra care**

**1. The index takes more than the raw vectors.**
A search index (the structure that makes searching fast) also stores links between vectors, the chunk text and metadata (extra fields like source or date). So real space is often well above vectors × dims × 4 bytes. Leave headroom, and check the service's own sizing guide or its reported usage.

**2. The numbers are stored smaller.**
Some services offer quantization, which means storing each number in 1 byte, or even less, instead of 4. Then the 4-byte rule overstates the size. Use the storage type you actually chose, and recheck quality on your eval set, since squeezing numbers can lose a little accuracy.

**3. Lots of searches, not just lots of data.**
Units cover storage, but heavy traffic may need replicas. A replica is an extra copy that shares the search load, and each one is billed too. Estimate searches per second as well as gigabytes. Also plan for growth, so you know when you'll cross the next step.

learn:term.a:
Without this idea, the search bill can triple and catch you by surprise.

Two quick terms first. A **chunk** is a small piece of a document, like a paragraph. A **vector** is the list of numbers a model turns that chunk into, so search can find chunks with similar meaning.

Here is a realistic case. Your team stores 2,000,000 chunks with `text-embedding-3-small`. That is about 12.3 GB. One Azure AI Search S1 unit holds 35 GB, so one unit is plenty. That costs about $245 a month.

Later someone switches to `text-embedding-3-large` for better quality. Each vector now has 3,072 numbers, twice as many. The documents also grow to 6,000,000 chunks. Now you need about 73.7 GB. That is 3 units, about $735 a month. Nobody planned for it.

The bill moves in whole steps, not smoothly. Each unit also bills every hour, even when nobody searches.

If you can do this sum, you see the jump coming. Then you can plan for it, or try shorter vectors first. Just check the answers stay good on your eval set (your test questions with known good answers).
